title: Utility Bill Audits: Eight Errors Worth Checking Every Month
summary: Late fees, estimated reads, wrong tariffs, and missed tax exemptions are common and recoverable. What a utility bill audit checks and how to automate. See how.
body_markdown:
Utility spend is one of the largest recurring costs for any multi-site organization, and one of the least checked. Most companies audit vendor invoices, travel expenses, and software contracts carefully. Utility bills are usually paid as they arrive, because checking them by hand means reading dozens of line items per bill, across many providers, every month.


A utility bill audit compares each bill against what it should be: the meter readings, the account's history, the applicable tariff, and the account's tax status. The errors it finds aren't rare edge cases. They're routine, they repeat until someone notices, and many of them are recoverable.


We see these errors on customer bills every month. Here are eight worth checking on every bill, how to spot each one, and how to make the checks automatic.


## The eight errors


### 1 Late fees and interest


Late fees are the simplest error and among the most common. They happen when a bill arrives at the wrong address, sits in a site manager's inbox, or waits in an approval queue. Interest on unpaid balances follows.


**How to spot it:** any late payment charge, interest charge, or past-due balance carried forward. Track them by account. Repeated late fees on the same account usually point to a broken delivery or approval path, not a one-off delay.


**What you can recover:** utilities will often waive a first late fee on request. The larger gain is prevention: fixing the bill delivery path and paying on time.


### 2 Estimated reads that run for months


When a utility can't read a meter, it estimates usage. One estimate is normal. A run of estimates over several months often ends with a large catch-up bill when an actual read finally happens, and in the meantime the account's costs and consumption data are wrong.


**How to spot it:** the read type on the bill, usually marked as "estimated" or with a code like "E." Flag any account with two or more consecutive estimated reads.


**What you can recover:** requesting an actual read early prevents a surprise catch-up bill, and in some cases it supports a rebilling request.


### 3 Usage spikes on estimated bills


A related problem: an estimated bill that shows much higher usage than the account's history. Estimates are sometimes based on the wrong period or a meter multiplier error.


**How to spot it:** compare estimated usage with the same month last year and the trailing average. A large jump on an estimated read deserves a call to the utility before the bill is paid.


**What you can recover:** the difference between the estimate and actual usage, through a corrected bill.


### 4 Charges on vacant or closed accounts


When a site closes or a building is vacated, utility accounts often keep billing. Customer charges, minimum charges, and fixed fees continue even at zero usage, and sometimes an account that should have been closed keeps receiving bills for months.


**How to spot it:** accounts with zero or near-zero usage for several consecutive months, and accounts at sites that are no longer active.


**What you can recover:** future charges, by closing the account properly. Some utilities will refund charges billed after a documented closing request.


### 5 Billed demand that doesn't match the site's load


Many commercial bills include demand charges based on the highest power draw during the billing period. Billed demand can exceed what the site drew because of minimum demand provisions, contract demand settings, or meter and multiplier errors.


**How to spot it:** compare billed demand with metered demand and with the site's historical peak. If interval data is available, check whether the billed peak appears in it at all.


**What you can recover:** overbilled demand charges from meter or multiplier errors; and, where contract demand is set too high, a lower setting going forward.


### 6 Low power factor penalties


Some utilities charge commercial and industrial customers when the site's power factor falls below a threshold set in the tariff. The penalty often appears as a separate line or as an adjustment to billed demand, and it repeats every month until the cause is fixed.


**How to spot it:** a power factor charge or adjustment on the bill, or a reported power factor below the tariff's threshold.


**What you can recover:** usually not past charges, since they're correctly billed under the tariff. The savings come from correcting the power factor, often with capacitor banks, which can pay back quickly at sites with recurring penalties.


### 7 Sales tax charged where an exemption applies


Many states exempt utilities used in manufacturing, processing, or by nonprofit organizations from sales tax, in whole or in part. Exemptions usually require a certificate on file with the utility, and they're often lost when accounts change hands or new accounts are opened.


**How to spot it:** sales tax charged on accounts at qualifying sites, or tax rates that differ between similar accounts in the same state.


**What you can recover:** future tax charges, by filing the certificate. Depending on the state and utility, overpaid tax from prior periods may be refundable.


### 8 The wrong rate schedule


Utilities offer several rate schedules for commercial customers, with different combinations of energy, demand, and time-of-use charges. Accounts are assigned a schedule when they're opened, and the assignment is rarely revisited, even when the site's usage pattern changes.


**How to spot it:** compare what the account would have paid over the last 12 months on each schedule it qualifies for. This requires both the account's usage history and the current tariffs.


**What you can recover:** lower costs going forward, by switching to the better schedule. In some cases a utility will rebill when an account was clearly placed on the wrong schedule.


Late fees, billing errors, and wrong tariffs are usually the fastest findings. A first audit of this kind typically recovers 1 to 3% of utility spend in the first quarter. Larger savings come later from rate optimization, demand management, and better budgeting.


Other issues are worth checking too: duplicate bills, overlapping billing periods, and charges for services the site no longer uses. A good audit covers all of them.


## Monthly checks vs. historical audits


There are two kinds of utility bill audit, and they work best together.


**Ongoing checks** run on every new bill before it's paid. They catch errors while they're still easy to fix: before a late fee, before a duplicate payment, before an estimate turns into a catch-up bill. This is where most of the prevention value is.


**A \[historical bill audit\](https://www.nectarclimate.com/feature/historical-bill-audit)** looks back across prior bills to find recoverable charges that were paid in error. It's a one-time project, usually covering one to three years of bills, and it often pays for itself through refunds and credits.
